title.narrative: Integrated response to the threat of Explosive Ordnance in Northern Ethiopia

description.narrative: Ethiopia has experienced a series of internal and international armed conflicts throughout its history, leaving a legacy of landmines and explosive ordnance (EO) scattered throughout the country. The outbreak of conflict in November 2020 between the central government and the regional authorities of the Tigray region, which spilled over into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions in 2021, has added new explosive contamination. Between August 2023 and August 2024, UNMAS was able to assess 67 woredas, which resulted in the identification and marking of 1,267 items of explosive ordnance, primarily consisting of grenades, rockets, mortars, projectiles, and air-dropped bombs. The results also show that estimated that 39% of woredas in Tigray and 25% in Afar regions are contaminated with some form of explosive ordnance. The new contamination adds to the estimated 726 square kilometres of legacy minefields from past conflicts. Based on the reports received through the Mine Action hotline, UNMAS teams will assess the impact of the threat on communities to inform mine action priorities and/or response in 15 woredas (9 in Tigray, 3 in Afar, 3 in Amhara). Based on the reports received through the Mine Action hotline, UNMAS teams will assess the impact of the threat on communities to inform mine action priorities and/or response in 15 woredas (9 in Tigray, 3 in Afar, 3 in Amhara).Explosive ordnance has a devastating impact on Ethiopians. Information collected and verified by UNMAS and Mine Action partners informs that in 2023 alone, a total of 1,584 victims of EO were recorded (77% casualties, 23% injured), with the majority being male (79%). In the first six months of 2024, 121 children represented an average of 74% of total victims recorded, indicating the high vulnerability of youngsters due to their lack of awareness of risks and often a tendency to play with unknown objects. While not all cases have been verified, it is believed that many more incidents remain unreported. Ethiopia's existing mine action capacity is insufficient to address the country's urgent needs, and there is limited data available to accurately assess the extent of the explosive threat. UNMAS deployed to Ethiopia initially upon request of the Ethiopian government to support the mapping of legacy contamination and subsequently to support broader mine action activities following the 2020-2022 conflict in Tigray. In parallel with the government’s request, the UN Resident/Humanitarian Coordinator asked UNMAS to provide mine action support to humanitarian operations in response to the crisis in northern Ethiopia. Since November 2023, UNMAS has had three field offices (two in the Tigray region and one in the Afar region) and its main office in Addis Ababa.UNMAS proposes a 12-month project to mitigate the threat posed by explosive ordnance through the:identification, registration and marking of EO in 15, previously unassessed woredas in Tigray, Afar and Amhara regions provision of Explosive Hazard Awareness Training (EHAT) to 250 humanitarian and development partners active in the EO affected regions/woredasdelivery of Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (EORE) to 600 people from communities confronted with explosive hazards
